A choropleth shades each region by a value — emissions, incidence, turnout, income. It is the most
common map in data analysis and the easiest to get *subtly wrong*: most "my map is all one colour"
complaints are not rendering bugs but scale bugs. CanvasXpress does the join and the colouring
inside the render, so in the browser you pass one value per region and a topoJSON of boundaries and
get an interactive, reproducible figure — and with the right colour scale it stays vivid on exactly
the kind of heavy-tailed data that flattens naive maps.

## First, the trap: colour encodes a *rate*, not a *count*

A choropleth fills an **area**, and area is a size channel your eye cannot help reading. Shade
regions by a raw count — total cases, total emissions, total sales — and big, populous regions light
up simply because they are big and populous. You have drawn a population map with extra steps. The
fix is almost always to map a **rate or density** (per capita, per 100k); reserve raw counts for a
proportional-symbol map, where a sized bubble carries the count honestly.

## The markup and the spec

The **columns** (`smps`) are the regions — they match the map by name — and the single **row**
(`vars`) is the variable you colour by: CO₂ emissions per country for 2018. We fetch a prepared
table and a small annotation table (continent, ISO code), parse the tab-separated text, and hand the
matrix to CanvasXpress. The two choices that make this map *work* are in the colour scale: a
seven-stop viridis `colorSpectrum`, and `colorSpectrumBreaksMethod: "quantile"`, which puts an equal
number of countries in every colour class — on skewed data that guarantee is what keeps all seven
colours on the map.

```html
<canvas id="co2quant" width="760" height="520"></canvas>
<script>
  var DATA = "https://www.canvasxpress.org/data/r/cX-CO2-dat.txt";
  var SMP  = "https://www.canvasxpress.org/data/r/cX-CO2-smp.txt";

  // split a tab-separated file into a list of cell-arrays (one per row)
  function rows(text) {
    return text.trim().split("\n").map(function (line) { return line.split("\t"); });
  }

  Promise.all([fetch(DATA).then(function (r) { return r.text(); }),
               fetch(SMP ).then(function (r) { return r.text(); })])
    .then(function (texts) {
      var d = rows(texts[0]);                      // [header, ["CO2", v1, v2, ...]]
      var countries = d[0].slice(1);               // header, minus the empty corner cell
      var values    = d[1].slice(1).map(Number);   // the CO2 values

      var s = rows(texts[1]);                       // header + one row per country
      var col = {};                                 // header name -> column index
      s[0].forEach(function (name, i) { col[name] = i; });
      var byCountry = {};
      s.slice(1).forEach(function (r) { byCountry[r[0]] = r; });
      var continent = countries.map(function (c) { return byCountry[c][col["Continent"] + 1]; });

      var data = {
        y: { vars: ["CO2"], smps: countries, data: [values] },
        x: { Continent: continent }
      };
      var config = {
        graphType: "Map",
        colorBy: "CO2",
        topoJSON: "https://www.canvasxpress.org/data/maps/WORLD.json",
        mapId: "co2Quantile",
        colorSpectrum: ["#440154", "#443983", "#31688e", "#21918c",
                        "#35b779", "#90d743", "#fde725"],
        colorSpectrumBreaksMethod: "quantile",
        mapColor: "#d9dde3",
        mapOutlineColor: "#ffffff",
        legendPosition: "bottom",
        title: "CO2 emissions per country (2018)",
        subtitle: "Seven quantile classes: each colour holds about 28 of 198 countries"
      };
      new CanvasXpress("co2quant", data, config);
    });
</script>
```

## Live result

```{=html}
<link href="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/neuhausi/canvasXpress@71.3.0/inst/htmlwidgets/lib/canvasXpress/canvasXpress.css" rel="stylesheet">
<script src="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/neuhausi/canvasXpress@71.3.0/inst/htmlwidgets/lib/canvasXpress/canvasXpress.min.js"></script>
<canvas id="co2quantLive" width="760" height="520"></canvas>
<script>
(function () {
  var DATA = "https://www.canvasxpress.org/data/r/cX-CO2-dat.txt";
  var SMP  = "https://www.canvasxpress.org/data/r/cX-CO2-smp.txt";
  function rows(text) {
    return text.trim().split("\n").map(function (line) { return line.split("\t"); });
  }
  function draw() {
    if (typeof CanvasXpress === "undefined") { return setTimeout(draw, 60); }
    Promise.all([fetch(DATA).then(function (r) { return r.text(); }),
                 fetch(SMP ).then(function (r) { return r.text(); })])
      .then(function (texts) {
        var d = rows(texts[0]);
        var countries = d[0].slice(1);
        var values    = d[1].slice(1).map(Number);
        var s = rows(texts[1]);
        var col = {};
        s[0].forEach(function (name, i) { col[name] = i; });
        var byCountry = {};
        s.slice(1).forEach(function (r) { byCountry[r[0]] = r; });
        var continent = countries.map(function (c) { return byCountry[c][col["Continent"] + 1]; });
        new CanvasXpress("co2quantLive",
          { y: { vars: ["CO2"], smps: countries, data: [values] }, x: { Continent: continent } },
          { graphType: "Map", colorBy: "CO2",
            topoJSON: "https://www.canvasxpress.org/data/maps/WORLD.json",
            mapId: "co2Quantile",
            colorSpectrum: ["#440154", "#443983", "#31688e", "#21918c",
                            "#35b779", "#90d743", "#fde725"],
            colorSpectrumBreaksMethod: "quantile",
            mapColor: "#d9dde3", mapOutlineColor: "#ffffff", legendPosition: "bottom",
            title: "CO2 emissions per country (2018)",
            subtitle: "Seven quantile classes: each colour holds about 28 of 198 countries" });
      });
  }
  draw();
})();
</script>
```

Every band of the ramp is doing work: the darkest purples are the smallest emitters, the yellows the
largest, and the legend's break values tell you the class edges are *data-driven*, not evenly spaced.
Hover any country for its name, continent and value.

## Why not just a plain linear ramp?

Because the data is **heavy-tailed** — a few countries emit thousands of megatonnes while most emit
almost nothing. On a linear scale, **195 of these 198 countries fall into the bottom fifth of the
range**, so a continuous ramp paints nearly the whole world one pale tone and spends its colour on
two or three outliers. See for yourself — same data, default scale:

```{=html}
<canvas id="co2linLive" width="700" height="480"></canvas>
<script>
(function () {
  var DATA = "https://www.canvasxpress.org/data/r/cX-CO2-dat.txt";
  function rows(text) {
    return text.trim().split("\n").map(function (line) { return line.split("\t"); });
  }
  function draw() {
    if (typeof CanvasXpress === "undefined") { return setTimeout(draw, 60); }
    fetch(DATA).then(function (r) { return r.text(); }).then(function (text) {
      var d = rows(text);
      var countries = d[0].slice(1);
      var values    = d[1].slice(1).map(Number);
      new CanvasXpress("co2linLive",
        { y: { vars: ["CO2"], smps: countries, data: [values] } },
        { graphType: "Map", colorBy: "CO2",
          topoJSON: "https://www.canvasxpress.org/data/maps/WORLD.json",
          mapId: "co2Linear", legendPosition: "left", theme: "solarized",
          title: "The same data on a plain linear ramp",
          subtitle: "195 of 198 countries sit in the bottom fifth of the scale - the map goes flat" });
    });
  }
  draw();
})();
</script>
```

This is the single most common choropleth failure. The cure is **classing**:

- `colorSpectrumBreaksMethod: "quantile"` — equal *counts* per class. Every colour is used, by
  construction. The right default for skewed data and for "which regions rank high/low" questions.
- `colorSpectrumBreaksMethod: "jenks"` — natural breaks that minimise within-class variance. Best
  when the data has genuine clusters with gaps between them; on smoothly heavy-tailed data like this
  it piles almost everything into the bottom class, so check the legend before you trust it.
- Three to seven classes is the usable range — beyond that, readers cannot match colours to the
  legend.

## Choose the palette on purpose

The palette is the scale's grammar, not decoration:

- **Sequential** (dark → light of ordered hues, like viridis above) for a quantity that only goes
  up: counts, rates, concentrations.
- **Diverging** (two hues meeting at a neutral midpoint) when values are meaningful *above and below
  a reference*: change vs. last year, difference from a target, a signed index. Use a three-colour
  `colorSpectrum` and pin the midpoint:

  ```js
  colorBy: "Change",
  colorSpectrum: ["#2166ac", "#f7f7f7", "#b2182b"],  // blue - neutral - red
  colorSpectrumZeroValue: 0                           // value mapped to the middle colour
  ```

  Never use a diverging palette for a purely positive quantity — the neutral midpoint invents a
  "normal" the data does not have. Viridis and the ColorBrewer ramps are colour-blind-safe and
  perceptually ordered; a rainbow ramp is neither. Keep the *same* scale across small multiples so
  maps stay comparable.

## Beyond the world map

- **Other boundaries.** Point `topoJSON` at any shape file — US states, a country's provinces,
  counties, custom districts. The join key is just the shape name.
- **Projection.** `mapProjection: "albers"` (equal-area) or `"mercator"`. Equal-area projections
  matter for choropleths: Mercator inflates high latitudes and exaggerates their visual weight.
- **Categorical maps.** Point `colorBy` at a categorical field for a qualitative choropleth with a
  discrete legend.
- **Polish.** `legendNumberFormat` formats the ticks, `legendInside` floats the legend over ocean,
  `showMapLabels` draws region names (best on few-region maps), `mapColor` sets the no-data fill so
  missing reads as missing, and `decorations` drops labelled markers on cities.

The whole figure — data, boundaries, classing rule and palette — is one portable spec you can
re-render from R or Python.
